name: SIG/BG
tagline: Which inputs separate signal from background, and which only appear to

intro.problem: The networks are only as good as their inputs, yet each input list was chosen before the current signal and background files existed. Some variables separate the samples because of physics; others separate them only because of how each sample was selected, and a ranking cannot tell the two apart on its own.
intro.value: A per-feature map of separation, region dependence and redundancy, with every selection effect flagged, gives the network-input work a trustworthy starting pool. It tells the barrel and endcap programs where the two regions carry different physics, and it hands the feature-competition game candidate sets that are already screened.
intro.approach: A public pipeline scores every shared column with the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance [@smirnov1948] per region and mass point, against its own noise floor; an Asimov expected-significance score [@cowan2011] with a permutation floor is next. Spearman correlation on background [@spearman1904] groups redundant features into blocks, and a gradient-boosted surrogate [@friedman2001] scores candidate input sets, with distance correlation [@szekely2007] between the two networks' surrogate scores.
intro.goals: A companion site where every plot is viewable and downloadable, the full development history is kept, and the excluded-feature list is editable; data-health checks that inform without removing features; and screened candidate pools handed to GAMBIT, which makes the final choice [@guyon2003].

questions: Which input variables separate signal from background in each region, and which only appear to because of how the samples were selected?
Where do the barrel and endcap differ in shape or in separation, so that a model trained in one region may carry the wrong physics into the other?
Which features are redundant with each other, and which strong separators do the current network input lists leave out?

components.name: Data health and inventory
components.subtitle: Block 00 · informational unit tests
components.summary: Every column in every input file is inventoried, duplicates are collapsed, exclusions are reported line by line, and the region split is audited. Data-health checks report pass or fail and never remove a feature; only the column rules (missing from a file, non-numeric, constant, duplicate, hard-excluded) drop one.

items.label: Selection
items.detail: A unit test checks the selection that defines each sample, because any variable tied to that selection separates the samples by construction

items.label: Exclusions
items.detail: One editable file of names or globs; the site can build a new one and download it

components.name: Separation and region maps
components.subtitle: Blocks A and B
components.summary: For each feature, the KS distance between signal and background in the endcap, the barrel and both, per mass point and combined with equal weight per mass point [@smirnov1948]. A separate map compares barrel and endcap shapes for background and for signal.

items.label: Noise floor
items.detail: Each distance is judged against the KS critical value for its sample sizes

items.label: Flags
items.detail: Selection-linked, jet-activity-dependent and non-physics features are marked in every ranking, and a feature that separates almost perfectly at a single mass point is marked suspicious

components.name: Correlation and candidate sets
components.subtitle: Blocks C and D · nominate, not decide
components.summary: Background rank correlation defines redundancy blocks [@spearman1904]. Four candidate input sets, from the current lists to an inclusive set, are scored by a gradient-boosted surrogate with five-fold cross-validation [@friedman2001]: separation per network role, the worst mass point, and dependence between the two roles [@szekely2007]. The surrogate nominates; GAMBIT decides on closure.

items.label: Hand-off
items.detail: Unit-test results, candidate pools per region, redundancy blocks, drop suggestions and the prototype lists, written as GAMBIT inputs

components.name: Companion site
components.subtitle: Public, static, every plot downloadable
components.summary: The site shows every feature page, ranking, correlation block and candidate set, every page of every PDF the work produced, and an archive of every earlier script version and run, unchanged. The code is public and runs on anyone's own copy of the files.

components.name: Scores for GAMBIT
components.subtitle: Next · score table and scoring layer
components.summary: A per-feature score table handed to GAMBIT: separation per region and mass point, an Asimov expected-significance score with a permutation noise floor [@cowan2011], surrogate drop-column change, redundancy block, selection flags and exclusion reason. Scores never gate a feature; they order GAMBIT's moves. They are computed on the selection half of a shared event split only, so the held-out half stays unseen. KS and Asimov are compared side by side, never blended into one number.

items.label: High and low
items.detail: High scores are discrimination candidates; clean low scores are candidates for shaping the background, since a feature with little signal information can still carry background structure

items.label: Weak features kept
items.detail: Clean features that separate poorly on their own stay in the pool; redundancy blocks keep their least selection-tied representative

items.label: Feedback
items.detail: GAMBIT's random partitions test which score predicts the end-to-end outcome; scores that predict nothing are demoted here in the next iteration

items.label: Scoring layer
items.detail: Binned Asimov first, against a permutation floor [@phipson2010]; then unbinned Asimov and Kullback–Leibler divergence [@kullback1951] on per-feature maximum-entropy densities from KERF [@jaynes1957]; the KS and Asimov orderings compared by rank concordance [@kendall1938]. The full design is on the sub-page

page.lede: KS distance sees differences in the bulk of a distribution and is nearly blind to its tails, where displaced-vertex quantities tend to live. An Asimov expected-significance score rewards purity wherever it occurs, tails included. This page describes the scoring layer that adds it: binned first, with a permutation noise floor, then unbinned on maximum-entropy densities from KERF. The scores are compared with KS, never blended, and they order GAMBIT's moves without ever gating a feature. Nothing here has run yet.

sections.heading: Why a second separation score
sections.text: KS is the largest gap between the two cumulative distributions, $D_{\mathrm{KS}}=\sup_x|F_s(x)-F_b(x)|$ [@smirnov1948]. A feature whose signal sits in a thin, nearly background-free tail moves the cumulative distributions very little, so it can rank low on KS and still make the best single cut. Expected significance measures that purity directly [@cowan2011].

sections.heading: Asimov per feature
sections.text: Each feature is histogrammed in bins of equal background weight, and the bins are combined as independent counting experiments: $Z_A^2=2\sum_i\big[(s_i+b_i)\ln(1+s_i/b_i)-s_i\big]$. For a small signal, $(1+r)\ln(1+r)-r\approx\tfrac12 r^2$, so $Z_A^2\approx\sum_i s_i^2/b_i=(S^2/B)\big(1+\chi^2(p_s\|p_b)\big)$. The ordering of features then does not depend on the unknown signal yield $S$: it ranks shapes by their $\chi^2$ divergence, and that yield-free divergence is reported beside $Z_A$.

items.label: Binning
items.detail: Edges at [[background-quantile|background quantiles]] with a minimum effective background count per bin, so no bin is empty of background. The outer bins are open, so signal beyond the background's range earns no extra credit

items.label: Background uncertainty
items.detail: A second column uses the form with a background uncertainty, set from the Monte Carlo statistics in each bin, which penalises thinly populated bins

items.label: Mass points
items.detail: Every mass point gets the same signal yield, so mass points weigh equally, as in the KS maps; the mean and the worst mass point are both reported

sections.heading: Noise floor
sections.text: KS has a critical value; Asimov does not. Signal and background labels are shuffled within each region and mass point, keeping counts and weights; the binning is redone and the score recomputed. Each feature is reported against the upper tail of that permutation distribution, with permutation p-values that are never zero [@phipson2010].

sections.heading: Maximum-entropy layer
sections.text: Histograms make Asimov depend on the binning. Step two replaces them with smooth per-feature densities for signal and background: [[maxent|maximum-entropy]] envelopes [@jaynes1957] supplied by KERF's Signal Line, imported here and never refit. The same densities give an unbinned $Z_A$ and the Kullback–Leibler divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_s\|p_b)=\mathbb{E}_s[\ln(p_s/p_b)]$, the expected log-likelihood ratio per signal event [@kullback1951].

items.label: Tails
items.detail: The divergence weights the regions where background is scarce, and there an envelope's tail comes from its functional form, not from data. The integrals stop where background statistics run out, and a tail-fraction column reports how much of each score comes from that region

items.label: Cross-fitting
items.detail: Densities are fitted on one fold and scored on the other, then swapped: fitting and scoring on the same events inflates every divergence

items.label: Shape-fit flag
items.detail: A feature that a smooth envelope cannot fit (discrete, spiky or sculpted by a cut) is flagged; like every flag here, it informs and never removes

items.label: Binned against unbinned
items.detail: Where the two Asimov scores disagree, the feature is flagged as sensitive to its binning or its tails

sections.heading: Compare, not blend
sections.text: KS, Asimov and KL are all functionals of the same pair of one-dimensional densities, so a weighted composite would add arbitrary weights and no information. The scores are read side by side.

items.label: Pareto front
items.detail: Per region and mass point, the features that no other feature beats on both KS and Asimov

items.label: Disagreement map
items.detail: High KS with low Asimov: separation in the bulk without purity, a shape input rather than a cut. High Asimov with low KS: separation in a low-background tail, which is the signature itself, a statistical fluke or a selection effect, and is inspected by hand

items.label: Rank concordance
items.detail: Kendall's $\tau$ between the two orderings, per region [@kendall1938]; a low value says the scores measure different things there, which is itself a finding

sections.heading: What it cannot see
sections.text: Every score here is marginal: one feature at a time. The networks use the joint distribution, and closure depends on dependence between feature blocks, which marginals do not carry. The gap between a feature's marginal rank and its weight in the surrogate points to interaction carriers and to redundant strong separators. Dependence itself is modelled in KERF and scored in GAMBIT.

items.label: Split rule
items.detail: Scores use only the selection half of the shared event split, assigned by a hash of event identifiers, so the held-out half stays unseen

items.label: Order, never gate
items.detail: Scores order GAMBIT's moves; only the column rules ever remove a feature

items.label: Record
items.detail: Specs and decisions are dated and append-only in the private repository; superseded scripts are archived, not overwritten

links.title: Feature competition
links.text: SIG/BG screens and nominates; GAMBIT takes the candidate pools and blocks and decides the partition. For GAMBIT's closure-blind design the scores become feedback: high scores order discrimination moves, clean low scores order moves that cut dependence between the networks, and GAMBIT's random partitions report back which scores predict the end-to-end outcome.

links.title: Barrel program
links.text: The barrel-versus-endcap maps show where the two regions carry different physics, which bears directly on pretraining a barrel model on the endcap.

links.title: Data-health checks
links.text: The informational unit tests here are the same kind of alert-not-stop checks BASELINE runs on its own files.

links.title: Maximum-entropy densities
links.text: KERF's Signal Line supplies the per-feature maximum-entropy signal and background envelopes behind the unbinned Asimov and KL scores. SIG/BG imports them and never refits them, so the two projects cannot drift apart.
